speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) what is the rate of medical inflation in Singapore over the past five years versus the global rate; (b) what is the projected rate of medical inflation for the next three years based on an expected increase in the goods and services tax in the near term; and (c) what is the Ministry doing to help bring down the rate of medical inflation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Healthcare inflation measures the growth rate of prices for healthcare related goods and services paid by patients after Government subsidies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Health)
text: While it is important to monitor healthcare inflation, it is just as important to look at overall healthcare spending.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This is because subsidies are funded from Government revenue, which comes from the people through taxes and duties and the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) from our Reserves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Hence, overall healthcare spending is a more complete indicator than healthcare inflation alone.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This requires the collective effort of all stakeholders to work together in close partnership.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These include initiatives to improve productivity through innovation and process improvements and working in collaboration with private sector and community providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Health)
text: MOH will continue to invest in this area and work closely together with our industry and community partners.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just one clarification with regard to medical inflation.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are many figures that are bandied around and, sometimes, this does cause unnecessary concern to the public.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It depends on where the source of the so-called medical inflation figures come from.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But just in terms of clarification, what figures does MOH use when they are looking at medical inflation?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Because a large part of expenditure is on private services, auxiliary or allied services, for example, even things like traditional Chinese medicine, which many members of our population actually make use of.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For allied health, for example, for an ageing population, what are people spending on daycare, for instance, or other services of this sort?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Dr Chia is right that it is important to not only focus on healthcare inflation but to look at the total healthcare spending.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, this is why when we look at it, how do we work on transforming the healthcare system to prevent healthcare costs from rising too quickly?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are not only focusing on healthcare inflation alone but we are taking a more complete view of how  we look at ways to help individuals stay healthy and how we look for ways to help our providers and our institutions deliver their services in a more productive and more efficient manner.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are also many other cost items that add up to the healthcare bill, for example, the cost of drugs and consumables.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, these are all different ways in which, I think, we will have to pay attention to.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Yesterday, in this House, we spoke about fee benchmarks.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Both Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Assoc Prof Goh raised questions about how we can best implement fee benchmarks.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In my answer, I explained that fee benchmarks and fee guidelines is part of a larger strategy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, it would also include some of these other measures.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: One last point I will make, Mr Deputy Speaker, is that, ultimately, whether we are able to effectively and successfully prevent healthcare costs from rising too quickly is not only what the Government can do alone, but what we can do together with our healthcare providers, our healthcare workers, our Labour Movement, our union leaders and also with patients and families.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This requires a collective effort from all of us.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is something that is important as we face an ageing population.
